briefing.question: Who may take a nation to war, and how does a republic hold its servants accountable?
briefing.agreed: Winning a war does not settle who had authority to wage it; impeachment must answer a breach of trust.
briefing.split: Madison, Congress decides war; Hamilton, energy and party danger; Aquinas, authority first; Locke, a revocable trust.

briefing.question: Who counts as a legitimate partner in governing, and should unity or mandate rule after a split verdict?
briefing.agreed: A split verdict is lawful, and the new government answers to those outside it too.
briefing.split: Madison, judge by rights kept; Mill, represent minorities; Rousseau, majority is not the general will; Schmitt, friend and enemy.

briefing.question: Where does responsibility lie between the individual who acts and the ideas and climate that shape him?
briefing.agreed: The killing is his alone to answer for; a whole camp does not carry his guilt.
briefing.split: Aristotle and Aquinas, habits and counsel share; Mill, only real incitement; Arendt, confront the stories that make enemies.

briefing.question: What are the limits of free expression, and is any subject off-limits to laughter?
briefing.agreed: No subject is legally off-limits, and context comes before judgment.
briefing.split: Aristotle, buffoon or boor; Hobbes, small glory; Aquinas, derision of grave evil is grave; Mill, defend it and keep one standard.

briefing.question: Where does political protest end and collective blame of a people begin?
briefing.agreed: Peaceful refusal to buy is legitimate; no one answers for belonging to a people.
briefing.split: Locke, deed or identity; Washington, no sanction to bigotry; Thoreau, conduct only; Gandhi, persuade, never frighten.

briefing.question: Who owns the memory of the dead, and what lessons may it be used to teach?
briefing.agreed: Remembrance teaches, and the dead belong to the whole people.
briefing.split: Pericles and Lincoln, a lesson large enough for all; Burke, keep the rite above policy; Nietzsche, both sides draw analogies.

briefing.question: Does the economy exist for people, or people for the economy, and what role should faith play in public life?
briefing.agreed: The economy exists for persons; inflation and destitution both wrong the poor.
briefing.split: Leo XIII, property with common use; Aquinas, just exchange; Smith, markets judged by the many; Hayek, teaching not planning.

briefing.question: How should an authoritative text be read across time, and who may exercise spiritual authority?
briefing.agreed: Scripture binds; the dispute is what kind of rule Paul gave and who confers office.
briefing.split: Luther, priesthood of all, office by call; Calvin, command or order; Wesley, extraordinary call; Vincent and Newman, growth or alteration.

briefing.question: How should a state balance the heritage and rights of a majority faith, the rights of minorities, and development?
briefing.agreed: The state may care for a holy city but may not favor or burden any faith.
briefing.split: Ashoka, reverence with concord; Ruskin, guard it for builders and pilgrims; Locke, civil not religious law; Madison, equal treatment.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Madison speaks first because the report names Federalist No. 51, ambition counteracting ambition, and because he wrote more than any founder on keeping the war power with the legislature. Hamilton answers him, since the report names his Federalist No. 70 on energy in the executive; his Federalist No. 69 and No. 65 also define the commander in chief and the impeachment power. Aquinas carries the just-war test the report names, legitimate authority and right intention. Locke wrote the first modern account of the federative power of war and peace, and of prudence where law cannot foresee. Grotius is left off because tonight's question is domestic authority and accountability, not the law between nations. The Secretary, the President, the House leaders, and the sponsor of the resolution are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: who may take a nation to war, and how does a republic hold its servants accountable? The report gives one side as supporters of impeachment, who say Congress holds the war power, and that a secretary who pursues hostilities without authorization, after voters punished the war at the midterms, must answer for it. The other side is his defenders, who say he has rebuilt readiness and won quick victories, that impeachment here is partisan theater, and that war strategy belongs to the elected commander in chief. Madison, you begin.

turn.text: We wrote the Constitution expecting that men would reach for power, and we built a counterweight into every office. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” (Federalist No. 51) The worst danger was that the sword, the purse, and the judgment of when to use them would gather in one place. “The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.” (Federalist No. 47)

turn.text: I told Jefferson in 1798 that the executive is the branch most interested in war and most prone to it, which is why the Constitution, with studied care, gave the question of war to the legislature (letters of 1798, paraphrased). So I would put the first question to Congress, not the Secretary. Did it authorize these hostilities, and if it did not, did it act when it learned of them? Impeachment is one of its instruments. But a Congress that lets the war power lapse for years and then reaches for impeachment after an election is also measured by my rule: ambition must counteract ambition, steadily, and not only when the vote is safe.

He would ask first whether Congress authorized these hostilities, and treat impeachment as a legitimate but late check if it did not.

turn.text: Madison is right about the text, and I said so myself. Of the President's command I wrote: “It would amount to nothing more than the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy; while that of the British king extends to the declaring of war and to the raising and regulating of fleets and armies--all which, by the Constitution under consideration, would appertain to the legislature.” (Federalist No. 69) But a republic that will not let its executive act will lose its wars and its liberty together. “Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government.” (Federalist No. 70) “Decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number” (Federalist No. 70) The Secretary's defenders lean on that argument, and it is a real one.

turn.text: On impeachment I was plainer than Madison about its dangers. It reaches political wrongs: “The subjects of its jurisdiction are those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust.” (Federalist No. 65) That is the right ground for the supporters to stand on. Whether hostilities were pursued without the authority the Constitution requires is an abuse of public trust if it is proved. But I also warned the other way: “there will always be the greatest danger that the decision will be regulated more by the comparative strength of parties, than by the real demonstrations of innocence or guilt” (Federalist No. 65) Energy in the executive does not license war without Congress, and impeachment is not a referendum on whether a war went well.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Aristotle speaks first because he wrote the first ethics of joking in Nicomachean Ethics IV, with a mean between the buffoon and the boor. Mill, named for the marketplace of ideas and the case that offense is not harm, closes on why even cruel speech should meet answers, not bans. Plato is left off because his worry was poetry's effect on the young, not the ethics of a joke about a real death. The comedian, the slain activist, and his widow are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: what are the limits of free expression, and is any subject off-limits to laughter? sittings.why_these_chairs: Leo XIII speaks first because the report names Rerum Novarum, the founding text of Catholic social teaching, which defends both private property and the claims of the poor. Aquinas, named for the just price, is the source Leo quotes on the common use of goods. Adam Smith, standing for the case that growth lifts the poor, wrote the invisible hand and insisted that no society of mostly poor people is flourishing. Hayek, named for the knowledge problem, is in copyright and is paraphrased only. Pius XI, who named subsidiarity, is left off because his 1931 encyclical is not a public-domain text tonight; Leo XIII's limits on the state carry the principle. The pope and the president are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: does the economy exist for people, or people for the economy, and what role should faith play in public life? The report gives one side as supporters of the pope, who say Catholic social teaching has long put human dignity and the poor before markets, and that the speech said so plainly. The other side is the president's defenders, who say free markets and property rights have lifted people out of poverty, that fiscal discipline ends the inflation that hurts the poor most, and that the Church should not prescribe economic policy. Leo XIII, you begin.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Luther speaks first because the report names the priesthood of all believers, which he set out in the Address to the Christian Nobility, along with the distinction between that priesthood and the public office. Calvin, standing for sola scriptura and the plain sense, wrote on Paul's rule about women's silence and on which church rules bind regardless of circumstance. Wesley, the nearest classic Protestant to this question in practice, allowed some women to preach under an extraordinary call; no fetched text of his letters was added tonight, so he is paraphrased. Vincent of Lérins gave the classic test of tradition, and Newman the classic account of how doctrine develops without becoming something else. Catherine Booth and Phoebe Palmer are left off because their defenses of women's preaching were not fetched tonight. The churches and their leaders are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: how should an authoritative text be read across time, and who may exercise spiritual authority? Those against ordination cite the letter to Timothy: “But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.” (1 Timothy 2:12) Those for it cite Galatians: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.” (Galatians 3:28) And Pentecost: “And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:17) The report gives one side as those for ordination, who cite the priesthood of all believers, women who led and taught in the New Testament, and gifting by the Spirit. The other side is those against, who cite passages such as 1 Timothy 2 and 3 and the historic practice of the church, and say fidelity to Scripture matters more than cultural pressure. Luther, you begin.

sittings.headline: Buddhist monks stage a sit-in over Sri Lanka's Anuradhapura redevelopment plan
sittings.question: How should a state balance the heritage and rights of a majority faith, the rights of minorities, and development?

setup.text: Monks are demanding withdrawal of a gazette that would expand the sacred area from 28 to 38 square kilometres. They cite a proposed fence around the Ruwanweli stupa and claims of new Hindu structures, which the planning department denies.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Ashoka speaks first because the report concerns a sacred city of Sri Lankan Buddhism, whose tradition traces its arrival to his mission, and his Rock Edict XII is the classic royal statement of honoring every sect. Ruskin, standing for the stewardship argument the report names, wrote the most famous case that old sacred buildings belong to past and future generations. Locke supplies the liberal principle of equal treatment and the line between religious and political law. Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance is the classic warning against a state favoring one establishment. Mircea Eliade, on sacred space, is left off because his work is in copyright and the turns here concern the state's duties, not the phenomenology of holy ground. The monks and the planning department are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: how should a state balance the heritage and rights of a majority faith, the rights of minorities, and development? The report gives one side as the monks, who say a site sacred to Sri Lankan Buddhism must be protected from changes that restrict worship or alter its character. The other side is the planning department, which says the plan adds conservation, pilgrim facilities, and infrastructure, and neither restricts pilgrims nor builds new religious structures. Ashoka, you begin.

turn.text: Ruskin speaks of stewardship; I would ask what kind of law this is.
